title: Saving a Tribe Through New Violence
overview: After nearly wiping out the tribe of Benjamin, the other tribes of Israel grieve the loss, then use a massacre and the kidnapping of young women to find wives for its few surviving men.

parts.label: Mourning a missing tribe (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: After the war in the previous chapter, only about 600 Benjamite men are left, so Israel weeps and offers sacrifices at Bethel, asking God why one of its twelve tribes is missing (vv. 2-4). Many readers note the irony: Israel's own war caused the loss, and Israel's own oath never to give a daughter to a Benjamite now blocks any recovery (vv. 1, 7).

parts.label: The attack on Jabesh Gilead (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Israel had also sworn to put to death anyone who skipped the gathering at Mizpah, and the town of Jabesh Gilead, east of the Jordan River, had sent no one (vv. 5, 8-9). Twelve thousand soldiers are ordered to kill every man, married woman and child there, and they bring back only 400 young women who had never slept with a man (vv. 10-12).

parts.label: Peace, and women handed over (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: Israel makes peace with the Benjamite survivors hiding at the rock of Rimmon and hands them the 400 women, but there are not enough for every man (vv. 13-14). The narrator explains the people's grief by saying the LORD had made a gap in the tribes (v. 15), a line many readers find uneasy beside a story in which Israel's own war and oaths caused the loss.

parts.label: A loophole at Shiloh (vv. 16-22)
parts.note: Still bound by their oath, the elders tell the remaining Benjamites to hide in the vineyards during a yearly festival of the LORD at Shiloh and seize the young women who come out to dance (vv. 16-21). If fathers or brothers complain, the elders will argue that no oath was broken because the families never gave their daughters away (v. 22, which translations word somewhat differently).

parts.label: Abduction and going home (vv. 23-24)
parts.note: The Benjamites do exactly this, each carrying off a dancing woman, and then rebuild their towns while the rest of Israel goes home. As with the women of Jabesh Gilead, nothing is said about what these women wanted, and the narrator offers no comment until the final line.

parts.label: No king in Israel (v. 25)
parts.note: The book ends with a refrain heard in its last chapters (see 17:6): Israel had no king, and everyone did as they saw fit. Many read this as the author's verdict on the chaos and a pointer toward Israel's coming kings, while others hear it as a judgment on a people who had stopped treating God as their king.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read the chapter's silence: older interpreters often treated parts of Israel's actions, such as the attack on Jabesh Gilead, as lawful punishment carried too far, while most modern readers see the whole episode as a deliberate portrait of a society's moral collapse.
think: What makes it possible for people to grieve one loss sincerely while causing new harm to others in their effort to repair it?
